conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal (or Postpartum) Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because mood and anxiety changes are incredibly common and we want to be sure you’re getting the care you deserve. Everything you share stays confidential between you and the clinical team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions that focus on the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment, and we can pause any time. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Oh—yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. My husband made a goofy face at the baby yesterday and we both cracked up. I guess it’s maybe not quite as easy as before she was born—like, I’m tired and distracted—but I can still find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yes, I still look forward to things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or taking her out in the stroller this afternoon. They’re small things, but they feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really—if the baby’s fussy or I’m running late, I just figure that’s part of having a newborn. I might think “oops, maybe I could’ve timed her nap better,” but I don’t sit around beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I do feel a little anxious, even when everything seems fine. Like, I’ll check if she’s breathing three or four times a night, or worry that a tiny cough means she’s getting sick, even though nothing’s really wrong. It’s not constant, but it pops up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky—just those little worries about her health, but nothing that makes my heart race or anything like that.
Things have been getting on top of me

A little bit. Some days the feed-diaper-nap cycle feels endless, and by dinner I’m thinking, “How is it already six o’clock and I haven’t brushed my teeth?” But it’s not overwhelming—just a bit piled-up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, not at all. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly. The baby wakes me, but my mood doesn’t keep me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable. Tired, yes, and maybe a little overwhelmed here and there, but not down or blue.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from feeling unhappy. I might tear up when a lullaby hits me just right, but it’s more sweet than sad.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 3: Screening note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) responses reviewed  (not a formal diagnosis):

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild, situational anxiety (items 4, 6): occasional nocturnal checking on infant, fleeting “piled-up” feeling by evening  
- No sustained low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, sleep-mood disruption, crying spells, or self-harm ideation (items 1–3, 7–10 negative)

Pattern  
- Preserved capacity for pleasure and laughter; stressors viewed as typical newborn challenges rather than personal failures  
- No pervasive dysphoria or functional impairment indicated

Risk screening  
- No current indicators for major depressive episode, generalized anxiety disorder, or safety concern (zero self-harm endorsement)  
- Reassure and continue routine postpartum monitoring; educate on normative anxiety and adaptive coping; return if mood worsens, enjoyment fades, or intrusive worries intensify
